nameStory: This spider earned its 'goldenrod' name because it's most commonly spotted hunting on bright yellow goldenrod flowers in late summer. The 'crab spider' part comes from its unusual ability to scuttle sideways like a beach crab, plus those front legs that it holds out wide like crab claws ready to snatch prey.
description: The goldenrod crab spider is a compact, stocky hunter that sits motionless on flowers waiting to ambush visiting insects. Females can reach up to 10mm (about the size of your pinky nail), while males are much smaller at only 5mm. They're usually bright white or sunny yellow, sometimes with pale green or pink tones, and have the remarkable ability to slowly change colors to match their flower perch.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Chunky, crab-like body with front two pairs of legs noticeably longer and thicker than the back pairs, held wide like a crab ready to grab

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Sits perfectly still on flower heads with front legs spread wide, can walk sideways and backwards as easily as forward

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Usually pure white or bright yellow, sometimes with faint stripes or bands on the abdomen, may show pale green or pink tints

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females are notably larger with chunky abdomens, while tiny males look almost like different species entirely

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web for hunting - these are ambush predators, though females leave silk draglines as they move between flowers

habitat: Look for these spiders on flower heads in sunny meadows, fields, and garden borders throughout New England. They particularly love goldenrod, milkweed, daisies, and other flat-topped flowers that provide a good hunting platform. You'll find them from sea level to mountain meadows, anywhere there are abundant flowering plants and the insects that visit them.

seasonality.spring: Young spiders are molting and growing, often found on early flowers like dandelions and wild cherry blossoms as they mature.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are hunting on summer flowers. Mating occurs and females begin selecting prime flower hunting spots.
seasonality.fall: Most visible on goldenrod and asters. Females lay eggs and guard their silk egg sacs until first frost, when they die.
seasonality.winter: Eggs overwinter in protected silk sacs. Adult spiders do not survive the cold New England winter.

funFact: These spiders are living mood rings - if they eat a lot of colorful prey like bright yellow bees or orange butterflies, their own bodies will gradually take on those same vibrant colors from their meals!
confusionNotes: Often confused with white or yellow jumping spiders, but crab spiders have that distinctive wide, crab-like stance with front legs spread wide, while jumping spiders sit more upright with legs tucked under. Memory trick: crab spiders sit like they're giving you a big hug with their front legs.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'goldenrod' crab spiders, they're actually found on dozens of different flower types and aren't restricted to goldenrod at all. The name stuck because goldenrod blooms when these spiders are most active and visible in late summer.
compareHints: This is the only Misumena species in New England, but it can be distinguished from other crab spiders in the region by its larger size and dramatic color-changing ability. Most other local crab spiders are smaller, duller, and stay the same color throughout their lives.
